analysis.one_liner: Requires safety testing, fuller ingredient labels, and recall authority for cosmetics and salon products.
analysis.headline: The bill won support from 26 House Democrats but never received a committee vote or a floor vote, dying in committee when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have, for the first time, put cosmetics under a legal safety standard: companies bringing products to market would have to register with the FDA and pay a fee, hand over safety data for public posting on a government website, and list every ingredient on the label, including what is currently hidden inside the word 'fragrance.' The FDA could then ban or restrict dangerous ingredients, test products for contaminants, and order recalls of unsafe products. It also required safety data sheets for professional salon products, written in languages salon workers can read, and pushed companies toward alternatives to animal testing.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers who use cosmetics every day, and especially the roughly hundreds of thousands of salon and nail-salon workers who are exposed to these products at high doses all day. The bill named them a vulnerable population, required safety data sheets for professional products in English, Spanish, Vietnamese, and other languages on request, and required companies to report serious health reactions. The FDA also gains, since it currently has almost no authority over cosmetic ingredients.

how_it_helps.text: Establishes a legal safety standard requiring 'reasonable certainty of no harm' for every cosmetic ingredient, accounting for cumulative exposure and vulnerable populations like pregnant women, children, and salon workers.

Requires annual registration and fees from companies with over $10 million in cosmetic sales, with the money reserved for oversight and enforcement, and exempts microbusinesses under $2 million in sales.
Requires every ingredient to be listed on the label, ends trade-secret protection for label ingredients, and forces internet sellers to post ingredient lists, including fragrance components.
Gives the FDA authority to order a recall or stop distribution of an adulterated or misbranded cosmetic, and requires companies to report serious adverse events within 15 business days.
Directs the Labor Department to issue a workplace safety standard requiring safety data sheets for professional-use salon products, available to employees in Spanish and Vietnamese on request.
Requires the FDA to minimize animal testing by preferring validated alternative methods.

analysis.who_pays: Large cosmetics and personal care companies, which would pay registration fees, submit all their safety data to a public database, disclose fragrance and other previously secret ingredients on labels, and reformulate or stop using any ingredient the FDA bans or restricts. Ingredient suppliers also face new contaminant testing and data-sharing duties. Small businesses above the $2 million microbusiness threshold would face registration paperwork, though technical support is provided.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large cosmetics makers and ingredient suppliers

drawbacks.text: The safety standard is extremely strict, targeting no more than a one-in-a-million lifetime risk and covering cumulative exposure from all sources, and requires labeling contaminants at levels as low as one part per billion, which could be technically difficult and force expensive reformulations or remove some products from the market.
Companies above $2 million in sales face annual registration, data submissions, and labeling changes, a real compliance burden even with the bill's small-business exemptions and technical support.
The bill creates new federal fees and directs unspecified appropriations for fiscal years 2014 through 2018, adding to federal spending on oversight.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is broad: cosmetics are one of the least-regulated categories of consumer products, and the people with the highest exposure, salon workers, have long lacked full safety information in a language they can read. The costs fall on large companies as fees, disclosure, and possible reformulation, which could show up in prices or reduced product choices. The strict one-in-a-million standard and part-per-billion contaminant labeling were the most contestable design choices, but the bill's carve-outs for microbusinesses and its fee structure focused the burden on the largest firms.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and then to subcommittees, and no committee ever took it up before the Congress ended, so it never reached the House floor for a vote.

narrative.text: Representative Jan Schakowsky introduced the bill on March 21, 2013, joined by 15 original cosponsors including Representatives Markey, Conyers, Ellison, and Grijalva, and 25 Democrats cosponsored in total.
The Speaker referred it to both the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Education and the Workforce Committee, a split referral that required both committees to act for the bill to move.
In the House, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health on March 22, 2013, and to the Education and Workforce Subcommittee on Workforce Protections on July 8, 2013.

No further action was ever recorded: there was no committee markup, no hearing recorded on the bill, no vote in either chamber, and the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 with the bill still sitting in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large cosmetics and personal care companies came out ahead: they never had to pay registration fees, disclose fragrance ingredients, submit safety data to a public database, or reformulate products around an FDA safety standard. Salon workers and consumers gained nothing, since the current weak-oversight system stayed in place.

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the bill's 26 supporters was a House Democrat, and no Republican cosponsored it; with both committees controlled by Republicans, it never advanced.

industries.industry: Large cosmetics and personal care product companies
industries.note: The bill would have charged them annual fees, made them disclose ingredients now hidden as trade secrets, publish their safety data, and reformulate anything the FDA bans or restricts. The current system, which leaves cosmetics essentially self-policed, is what remained in place.
Suppliers would have had to test ingredients for listed contaminants and hand over safety specifications and data to manufacturers on request, with failure made a federal offense.

Salon workers, a heavily female and immigrant workforce, would have gained guaranteed access to safety data sheets in Spanish and Vietnamese; salon owners face modest paperwork duties but were not among those paying fees.

Microbusinesses under $2 million in sales were exempt from registration and fees, and firms under $10 million paid no fee, but companies in between still faced registration and data rules, cushioned by promised technical support.
